title: Connexions de Gauss-Manin et équations de Picard-Fuchs. Opération de Cartier : copies de tapuscrit annoté (s.d.), tiré à part (1981), notes manuscrites (s.d.).

deep.reconstruction:
Setting, from the neighbouring pages: X -> S is a smooth family of (complex-analytic) curves. It carries a connection in the geometric sense: a way of lifting a differential operator D on S to an operator D-bar acting on functions and relative forms on X. A finite family of relative 1-forms omega_i and operators D_i on S is given. Grothendieck is proving a criterion for a Picard-Fuchs type relation. Condition (7) is that the 'lifted' combination varpi = sum D-bar_i omega_i is locally (over S) relatively exact, varpi = d phi as in (10). This condition should imply the Picard-Fuchs relation (3): sum_i D_i int_{Z_s} omega_i = 0 for all cycles Z_s.

The key tool is the 'differentiation under the integral sign' formula (12): D_s int_{Z_s} omega_s = int_{Z_s} (D-bar omega)_s. On this page he reduces (12) to a statement about paths, in four steps.
1. Decompose the cycle Z_{s0} into small paths a_i -> a_{i+1} (a wavy path is sketched).
2. Transport the subdivision points a_i horizontally, i.e. as horizontal sections of the connection, near s0.
3. Prove the more general formula (3): D_s int_{a(s)}^{b(s)} omega_s = int_{a(s)}^{b(s)} (D-bar omega)_s whenever the endpoints a(s), b(s) are horizontal sections. A N.B. generalises this to (3 bis), for differentiably varying 1-chains C_s whose boundary is horizontal.
4. Proof of (3): work near s0 with a(s0), b(s0) close together, so that on a neighbourhood in X one has omega = d phi (relative Poincare lemma). The left side then becomes D_s(phi(b(s)) - phi(a(s))). The next page finishes the argument: D-bar commutes with relative d, so the right side is (D-bar phi)(b(s)) - (D-bar phi)(a(s)). The two sides agree because, for b horizontal, D_s(phi(b(s))) = (D-bar phi)(b(s)), essentially the chain rule.

The next page also notes the converse use. For horizontal endpoints, mu(a,b) = int_a^b sum D-bar_i omega_i = phi(b) - phi(a). So the Picard-Fuchs operator applied to an incomplete integral between horizontal sections yields the explicit 'boundary' function phi(b(s)) - phi(a(s)). The purpose is a down-to-earth, analytic proof that relative exactness of the lifted combination gives Picard-Fuchs equations, in the course of explaining the Gauss-Manin connection.
errors: For higher-order D (or several D_i), the identity D_s(phi(b(s))) = (D-bar phi)(b(s)) needs D-bar to be a multiplicative lifting of differential operators, i.e. an integrable connection. This is not stated on this page; it may be stated earlier.

Gap: the commutation of D-bar with the relative differential d, and the existence of the local primitive phi on an open subset of X (not just on a fibre), are used without comment. Both are standard for a horizontal lift and a relative Poincare lemma on small neighbourhoods.
Minor: on the previous page, int over the boundary of Z_s of phi = 0 is asserted with a [?]. It is correct since Z_s is a cycle.

ideas.what: Differentiation of period integrals under the integral sign via a horizontal lift: D_s int_{Z_s} omega = int_{Z_s} D-bar omega
ideas.modern_name: Gauss-Manin connection computed via Ehresmann connection / Lie derivative of horizontal lifts
ideas.usually_credited_to: Classical (Picard, Fuchs); modern form Manin 1958, Katz-Oda 1968
ideas.where_published: Possibly the related tapuscrit on Gauss-Manin connections in this same cote

ideas.what: Extension to paths with horizontally moving endpoints, and to chains with horizontal boundary (3 bis)
ideas.modern_name: Gauss-Manin connection on relative homology H_1(X_s, {a(s), b(s)}); periods of relative cycles
ideas.usually_credited_to: Classical (incomplete abelian integrals); Manin's kernel-theorem setting

ideas.what: Picard-Fuchs operator applied to an incomplete integral between horizontal sections equals phi(b) - phi(a), where phi is the primitive of the lifted combination
ideas.modern_name: Inhomogeneous Picard-Fuchs equations for abelian integrals with moving endpoints (Manin map)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Manin (1963, Mordell conjecture over function fields)

deep.surprise_reason: This is a careful but standard proof of differentiation under the integral sign for periods, extended to paths with horizontal endpoints. Everything is classical: Picard-Fuchs, Gauss-Manin, incomplete abelian integrals as in Manin. Nothing a specialist would find new.
transcription_corrections: '$\xi$]' in line 3 is probably part of the closing of the bracketed remark (an 'etc.' or similar), not a variable.
The underlined phrase in the middle is 'sections horizontales pour la connexion'.
The inserted line reads 'se plaçant au voisinage de s_0 et' and is boxed or underlined as an insertion.
Near the bottom: 'Mais alors le premier membre est D_s(phi(b(s)) - phi(a(s))), le ...'. The left-hand side is meant; the phrase continues onto the next page with 'comme on a ...'.
The equation label written as (3) on this page is likely (13) (it looks like '(1 3)'). The next page's numbering (14) supports '(13)' and '(13 bis)'.
